stages.title: What is a story?
stages.hook: Think of a tale someone told you. Who was in it, and what happened?
explain: A story tells about things that happen. It can be real or made up. Stories have people or animals in them. Things happen to them.
We hear stories, read stories and tell stories. Some stories are in books. Some are told out loud. People all over the world love stories.
A story makes pictures in your head. It can make you laugh. It can teach you something new.

example.q: Tell a tiny story: a duck lost its hat.
steps: Who is in it? A duck.
What happens? The duck loses its hat.
A story needs someone and something that happens.
example.a: A duck loses a hat. That is a tiny story.

analogies.home: Bedtime stories are told at home when it is quiet and cosy.
analogies.city: A library has many shelves full of stories to borrow.
analogies.farm: A farmer might tell a story about a clever hen.
analogies.nature: Grandparents may tell a story under a big tree.

stages.mnemonic: A story is a train: someone gets on, something happens, and off it goes.
terms: Something that tells what happens to someone.
The person who writes a story.
To say a story out loud.

misc.wrong: A story must be in a book.
misc.right: A story can be in a book, or told out loud, or acted out. Many old stories were told by voice first.

trip.prompt: Look at the picture of people telling stories. Where are they sitting?

questions.q: Which one is a story?
o: A fox finds a lost mitten and gives it back.
Red, blue and green paint pots all lined up on a shelf.
One, two, three, four, five, six.
A chair, a table and a bed.
questions.why: A story tells what happens to someone. The other choices are only lists.

questions.q: How can we share a story?
o: By hiding it under a big bed
questions.why: Stories can be told out loud, written, or shown in pictures.

questions.q: Who writes a book story?
questions.why: The author is the person who writes the story.

questions.q: A story can be made up.
questions.why: Many stories are made up, like tales about talking animals.

questions.q: What does a story need to have?
o: Only a very long list of numbers
questions.why: A story needs a who and a what happened.

questions.q: Mia says: "A cat sat. Then it chased a bird up a tree." Is this a story?
o: Yes, something happens to the cat
No, cats cannot be in stories
No, it is too short to be anything
Only if it has a picture
questions.why: Even short tellings are stories if someone does something.

questions.q: Put these in order to tell a tiny story.
questions.why: First the seed is planted, then it grows, then she picks the flower.

questions.q: Match each to its job.
questions.why: An author writes, a listener hears, a book holds words.

questions.q: Why do people like stories?
o: They can feel, imagine and learn
They make you grow much taller overnight
questions.why: Stories help us feel, imagine and learn.

questions.q: Grandpa tells a story with no book. How is the story shared?
o: By a song with no words
questions.why: Telling out loud is called oral storytelling.

panel.q: Why do you think stories are told in every country?
o: People everywhere enjoy sharing ideas and feelings
Only one country made stories long ago, and kept them
Stories are only for school days
panel.why: Stories are found in all cultures because people everywhere like to share.

panel.q: A story has no one in it and nothing happens. What is wrong?
o: It is missing who and what happens
It has too many colourful pictures
It has no cover on the front
panel.why: Without someone or events there is no story.

panel.q: Why is an old story still told today?
o: People keep telling it to each other
It was hidden away and then it was forgotten
panel.why: Stories travel because people share them again and again.

teach.model: A story tells what happens to someone. It can be made up or real. It has a person or animal, and something happens. You can hear it, read it or see it. For example, a bear finds honey.

stages.title: Characters and settings
stages.hook: Where does a story happen, and who is in it?
explain: Characters are the people or animals in a story. A setting is where and when the story happens, like a forest, a farm or a ship.
A character can be kind, brave, funny or shy. The setting can be sunny, dark, hot or snowy.
When you tell a story, say who is in it and where they are.

example.q: Who and where: a rabbit hops in a snowy garden.
steps: Who is the character? A rabbit.
Where is the setting? A snowy garden.

analogies.home: The kitchen is a setting. Your family are the characters.
analogies.city: A bus stop can be a setting for a story.
analogies.farm: A barn is a setting. The hen is a character.
analogies.sea: A boat on the waves is a setting.

stages.mnemonic: Characters are WHO. Setting is WHERE.
terms: A person or animal in a story.
Where and when a story happens.

misc.right: The setting is the place, not a person. People and animals are characters.

trip.prompt: Look for different kinds of characters.

questions.q: What is a character?
o: The last page of the book
questions.why: Characters are the people or animals in the story.

questions.q: What is a setting?
questions.why: Setting means the place and time.

questions.q: A hen lives in a barn. Which is the setting?
questions.why: The barn is the place.

questions.q: A turtle swims in the sea. Which is the character?
questions.why: The turtle is the one the story is about.

questions.q: Which could be a setting?
questions.why: A mountain is a place.

questions.q: A story is set in a cold snowy land. Which character fits best?
questions.why: A polar bear lives in snow and ice.

questions.q: Match each to what it is.
questions.why: People and animals are characters. Places are settings.

questions.q: Can a story have more than one character?
questions.why: Many stories have many characters.

questions.q: If we change the setting from a desert to the ocean, what changes?
o: Who wrote the whole story down
questions.why: Setting is the place, so it changes the place.

questions.q: Why tell the setting?
o: So listeners can picture the place
To make the story much longer and longer
questions.why: A setting helps us imagine.

panel.q: A story is about Kofi at a market in Accra. What is the setting?
o: Kofi, the boy in the story

panel.q: Why do the same characters feel different in a new setting?
o: The place changes what can happen
They are all given brand new names
panel.why: A new setting changes the problems and the fun.

panel.q: A character is shy. How might they act?

teach.model: Characters are the people or animals in a story. The setting is where the story happens. A bird in a tree is a good example: the bird is the character and the tree is the setting.

stages.title: Beginning, middle and ending
stages.hook: Every story starts somewhere and stops somewhere. What happens in between?
explain: A story has a beginning, a middle and an ending. The beginning tells us who and where. The middle has a problem or an adventure. The ending tells how things turn out.
Think of a sandwich: bread, filling, bread. The middle is the exciting part.
When you retell a story, try to say first, next and last.

example.q: The three little steps: a boy loses his kite, looks for it, finds it in a tree.
steps: Beginning: the boy loses his kite.
Middle: he looks and looks.
Ending: he finds it in a tree.
example.a: Beginning: kite lost. Middle: search. Ending: kite found.

analogies.home: Getting ready for bed has a beginning, middle and end: pyjamas, story, sleep.
analogies.city: A bus ride starts at one stop, goes along, and ends at another.
analogies.farm: A seed is sown, it grows, and then we harvest.
analogies.nature: A caterpillar, a cocoon, a butterfly.

stages.mnemonic: First, Next, Last: a story walks in three steps.
terms: The part with the problem or adventure.

misc.wrong: The ending is where the story starts.
misc.right: The ending is the last part. The beginning is the first.

trip.prompt: Find the parts of a story shape.

questions.q: What comes first in a story?
questions.why: Stories start with the beginning.

questions.q: Where do we find out how things turn out?
questions.why: The ending tells how it all turns out.

questions.q: Which part usually has the problem or adventure?
questions.why: The middle is where the trouble happens.

questions.q: Put the story in order.
questions.why: Wake, cook, then eat.

questions.q: Order the seed story.
questions.why: Plant, grow, bloom.

questions.q: A story starts with a girl who lost her ball. Which is likely the ending?
o: She finds the ball and plays
She wakes up in her bed
The ball is red, round and old
questions.why: An ending solves the problem.

questions.q: What if a story has no ending?
o: We do not know what happens
It becomes a perfect story for ever
questions.why: Without an ending we are left wondering.

questions.q: Which tells us who and where?
questions.why: The beginning introduces characters and setting.

questions.q: The words "Once upon a time" usually start...
questions.why: They are a classic way to begin a tale.

questions.q: Why do we need a middle?
o: It uses up more of the paper
questions.why: Without a middle there is no adventure.

panel.q: Sam starts a story with the ending. What might the listener feel?
o: Puzzled, and want to know how it got there
Happy, as if nothing is missing from it at all

panel.q: Why do many stories end with a solved problem?
panel.why: A solved problem leaves listeners satisfied.

panel.q: Which is the best way to retell a story?
panel.why: Following the order keeps the story clear.

teach.model: A story has three parts. First is the beginning. Next is the middle with the problem. Last is the ending. For example, a lost kite is found.

stages.title: Simple folktales
stages.hook: Have you heard of a clever spider who tricks big animals? Who might tell such a tale?
explain: A folktale is a very old story that people tell again and again. Nobody knows who first told it. Families share them out loud.
Folktales come from every part of the world. Anansi the spider comes from the Akan people of Ghana. In the story he is small but very clever.
Folktales often have animals that talk. They often teach us something kind or wise.

example.q: Anansi and the pot of wisdom: Anansi tries to keep all wisdom to himself.
steps: Anansi gathers all wisdom in a pot.
He tries to hide it high in a tree.
He cannot climb well with the pot in front, and the pot falls and wisdom spreads to everyone.
example.a: The wisdom is shared with everyone, so no one person can keep it all.

analogies.home: Folktales are told by grandparents at home.
analogies.city: Storytellers visit libraries to share folktales.
analogies.farm: Farmers tell tales by the fire after work.
analogies.nature: Many tales have animals from the forest.

stages.mnemonic: Folk means people. Folktales are the people's tales.
terms: An old story passed on by people.
A clever spider in Akan stories from Ghana.

misc.wrong: Folktales were all written by one person.
misc.right: Folktales were passed on by many tellers, usually by mouth, over a long time.

stages.limits: Tellers tell the same tale in different ways.

trip.prompt: Look for tales from different places.

questions.q: Where does Anansi the spider come from?
o: The cold lands of the North Pole
questions.why: Anansi stories come from the Akan people of West Africa.

questions.q: What is a folktale?
o: An old story told by many people
A shopping list for the market on Monday
questions.why: Folktales are old stories that people pass on.

questions.q: How were many folktales first shared?
o: By email, sent from far away
questions.why: Before books people told stories by mouth.

questions.q: Anansi is small but...
questions.why: Anansi uses his wits.

questions.q: Folktales can have...
questions.why: Talking animals are common.

questions.q: Does only one country have folktales?
o: No, every part of the world has them
Yes, only one country in the world has them
questions.why: All peoples tell folktales.

questions.q: Two tellers tell the same folktale a bit differently. Why?
o: They remember and add in their own way
One of the tellers is wrong, so they must stop
The tale has lost its ending
questions.why: Spoken tales change a little with each teller.

questions.q: A folktale says the small spider tricks a big beast. What idea might it teach?
o: Cleverness can matter more than size
Big is always the best way to win a fight
questions.why: Many trickster tales celebrate cleverness.

questions.q: Match the tale to a thing.
questions.why: These match the lesson.

questions.q: Why is it good to name where a folktale is from?
o: It shows respect to the people who told it
It makes the tale shorter and quicker to tell
questions.why: We honour the people whose tale it is.

panel.q: Why do folktales often teach lessons?
o: They help families share what they value
They are tests that children must pass at school
They are rules for a game
panel.why: Lessons are a way to share values.

panel.q: A tale has a clever spider who shares wisdom. What does the pot falling suggest?
o: Clay pots are heavy to carry

panel.q: Why might a folktale last for hundreds of years?
o: People enjoy it and keep telling it
It is carved in stone and never moves

teach.model: A folktale is an old story told by many people. It often has animals who talk. Anansi the spider from the Akan people of Ghana is clever. Tales teach us gentle lessons.

points.ask: Who is a character in one?

stages.title: Fables and moral lessons
stages.hook: Can a slow animal win a race? What would that teach us?
explain: A fable is a short story with animals that act like people. At the end there is a lesson called a moral.
Aesop told many fables long ago in ancient Greece. In The Tortoise and the Hare, the hare is fast but naps. The tortoise keeps going and wins.
The moral is that steady effort can beat quick but careless play.

example.q: Find the moral: The Boy Who Cried Wolf.
steps: A boy shouts "wolf" as a joke.
People run to help and see there is no wolf.
Later a real wolf comes and nobody believes him.
example.a: Moral: if you tell lies, people may not trust you when you tell the truth.

analogies.home: A fable at home might teach us to share our toys.
analogies.city: Short fables can be heard on a bus ride.
analogies.farm: Fables often have farm animals like geese and foxes.
analogies.sport: In a race the tortoise reminds us to keep going.

stages.mnemonic: A fable is a short tale; the moral is the tail at the end.
terms: A short story with animals that teaches a lesson.
A storyteller from ancient Greece known for fables.

misc.wrong: A moral is the name of a character.
misc.right: A moral is the lesson, not a character.

questions.q: What is a moral?
questions.why: The moral tells what we learn.

questions.q: In The Tortoise and the Hare, who wins?
questions.why: The tortoise keeps going and wins.

questions.q: Fables often have animals that...
questions.why: They talk and think like humans.

questions.q: Who is Aesop linked to?
questions.why: Aesop's name goes with many fables.

questions.q: What lesson does The Tortoise and the Hare give?
questions.why: The hare was careless.

questions.q: The Boy Who Cried Wolf teaches us...
questions.why: Lies lose trust.

questions.q: Lena shares her lunch with a hungry friend, and later the friend helps her. Which moral fits?
questions.why: Kind acts can return.

questions.q: Order The Boy Who Cried Wolf.
items: The boy shouts about a wolf as a joke
The villagers run to help and see no wolf
questions.why: He lies first, then trust is lost when it matters.

questions.q: In the Lion and the Mouse, the small mouse helps the big lion. What is the moral?
o: Lions are weak and small animals
questions.why: Kindness to the small can be repaid.

questions.q: Why do fables use animals?
o: It makes lessons easy and fun to remember
Because people can never be in any stories
Animals wrote them down long ago
questions.why: Animals can stand for human habits.

panel.q: A hare brags and sleeps, and a tortoise wins. Is the story saying slow is always better?
o: No, it says careless boasting can lose
Yes, slow always wins every single race
panel.why: The point is about effort and carelessness.

panel.q: Why are fables short?
panel.why: A short tale keeps the moral clear.

panel.q: A fable ends with: "Do not count your chickens before they hatch." What is that?

teach.model: A fable is a short story with animals. The animals act like people. At the end there is a moral, which is a lesson. For example, the tortoise wins by not giving up.

stages.title: Rhymes and poems
stages.hook: What words sound the same at the end? Cat, hat... what else?
explain: A poem uses words in a special way. Many poems have rhyme: words that end with the same sound, like cat and hat.
Poems have a beat, a bit like a drum. Clap along to the words. Poems can be short and funny or soft and sweet.
Nursery rhymes are short poems for children. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star" is a very old one that many people know.

example.q: Find the rhyme: moon, spoon, sun.
steps: Say each word slowly.
Moon and spoon end the same: -oon.
Sun does not.

analogies.home: Rocking a baby to a rhyme.
analogies.city: A street seller singing a rhyme.
analogies.music: A rhyme can be sung or clapped.
analogies.nature: The rain says pitter-patter, a rhyming sound.

stages.mnemonic: Rhymes chime like bells at the end of the line.
terms: Words arranged with beat and care.
Words that end with the same sound.
The steady pulse of a poem.

misc.right: Many poems rhyme but not all do. Some use only rhythm and pictures.

trip.prompt: Look for a rhyme you know.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with cat?
questions.why: Cat and hat end in -at.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with moon?
questions.why: Moon and spoon share -oon.

questions.q: What is a rhyme?
o: Words with the same ending sound
Words that start the same way each time
questions.why: Rhymes match at the end.

questions.q: What is a beat?
questions.why: The beat is the rhythm we clap.

questions.q: Which pair rhymes?
questions.why: Bee and tree end the same.

questions.q: Which is a nursery rhyme?
o: A bus timetable for the town centre
questions.why: It is a very old rhyme for children.

questions.q: Match rhymes.
questions.why: Each pair has the same end sound.

questions.q: Does every poem have to rhyme?
questions.why: Some poems use only rhythm and images.

questions.q: Why do rhymes help us remember?
o: The sounds and beat are easy to repeat
They are very, very long and very loud
questions.why: Pattern helps memory.

questions.q: You want a rhyme for "pie". Which will do?
questions.why: Pie and sky end in the same -ie sound.

panel.q: Why might a poem about rain use a quick, tapping beat?
A poem has no rhyme. Is it still a poem?
o: Yes, it can use beat and pictures
No, it is never a poem without a rhyme
Only if it is very long

panel.q: Why do poems often use few words?
o: Each word is chosen with care
They run out of ink fast
Words cost lots of money to buy

teach.model: A poem is made of words with beat. A rhyme is when words end with the same sound, like cat and hat. Poems can be sung or clapped. Not every poem has rhyme.

stages.title: Storytelling through pictures
stages.hook: Can you tell a story without any words at all?
explain: Pictures can tell stories too. Look at three pictures in a row: a seed, a sprout, a flower. You know the story already!
Many books for young children have lots of pictures. Some have almost no words. Comics also use pictures in boxes to show what happens.
People have told stories with pictures for thousands of years. Some paint on walls, some on cloth and some on bark.

example.q: Read the pictures: a cloud, rain, a puddle with a boy jumping.
steps: The cloud comes first.
Then rain falls.
Then the boy jumps in the puddle.
example.a: A rainy day ends with a fun puddle jump.

analogies.home: A photo album tells the story of your family.
analogies.city: Signs use pictures so everyone can understand.
analogies.nature: Cave paintings show animals people saw long ago.
analogies.tech: Emoji are tiny pictures that tell a feeling.

stages.mnemonic: Pictures are words you see with your eyes.
terms: A picture that goes with a story.
A story told in boxes of pictures.
Things in order, one after another.

misc.wrong: You need words to tell a story.
misc.right: Pictures alone can tell a whole story if we look at them in order.

trip.prompt: Find pictures that tell a story.

questions.q: Can a story be told with pictures only?
questions.why: Many picture books have no words.

questions.q: What is an illustration?
o: A picture that goes with a story
A loud sound in the street at night
questions.why: Illustrators draw them.

questions.q: What are the boxes in a comic for?
questions.why: Each box shows a step.

questions.q: Order the pictures.
questions.why: The seed grows into a flower.

questions.q: Order the picture story.
questions.why: Cloud, rain, then rainbow.

questions.q: A picture shows a girl with a wide smile holding a medal. How does she feel?
questions.why: Faces and objects give clues.

questions.q: Why look at the picture's small details?
o: They give clues about the story
They are not important at all, really
questions.why: Details show who, where and how.

questions.q: Who draws the pictures in a book?
o: A bus driver in the town
questions.why: Illustrators make pictures for books.

questions.q: Why might a sign use a picture instead of words?
o: Many people can understand it quickly
Pictures are cheaper to print than words
questions.why: Pictures work across languages.

questions.q: Long ago people painted animals on cave walls. What does that suggest?
o: People used pictures to share things
They had cameras to take their pictures
questions.why: Pictures were one of the first ways to share.

panel.q: A picture book shows a boy getting smaller and smaller as the wall behind gets bigger. What might the artist show?
panel.why: Artists use size to show feelings.

panel.q: Why is the order of pictures important?
o: It tells what happens first and last
It does not matter at all which comes first
It gives the page its colours

panel.q: Two people tell different stories from the same picture. Is that okay?
o: Yes, we can imagine different things
No, only one person is right
No, pictures cannot be used for stories

teach.model: Pictures can tell stories. We look at them in order. A seed, a sprout and a flower tell how a plant grows. Artists give clues in faces and colours.

stages.title: Listening to stories
stages.hook: What does a good listener do when a story is told?
explain: Listening is part of a story. A good listener sits still and uses eyes and ears. A good listener thinks about who and where.
You can ask questions after the story: Who was in it? What happened? How did it end?
Listening helps you learn new words and ideas. Many families keep their stories by telling them out loud.

example.q: Listen and answer: "A fox found a drum. It banged it and scared the crows away."
steps: Who? A fox.
What happened? It found a drum and banged it.
The crows flew away.
example.a: The fox scared the crows with a drum.

analogies.home: Listen to a bedtime story with your family.
analogies.city: Listen to the library story hour.
analogies.farm: Listen to a farmer's tale by the fire.
analogies.music: Listening to a song uses the same careful ears.

stages.mnemonic: Ears open, mouth closed, eyes bright: listen right!
terms: To pay attention to sounds and words.
Something we ask to learn more.

misc.right: Listening is active: we think, picture and remember.

trip.prompt: Find who keeps stories by telling.

questions.q: What does a good listener do?
questions.why: Good listeners focus.

questions.q: Which body part helps us listen?
questions.why: We hear with our ears.

questions.q: After a story, which question helps?
questions.why: It checks that we understood.

questions.q: What is oral storytelling?
o: Painting a story on a wall
Cooking a story in a pot
questions.why: Oral means spoken.

questions.q: A teller says "a big, grey elephant walked by". What do you picture?
o: A tiny red ant on a leaf
questions.why: Listening makes pictures in your head.

questions.q: Why is it kind to listen to a storyteller?
questions.why: Listening shows we care.

questions.q: Order a good listening routine.
questions.why: First sit, then listen, then ask.

questions.q: If you do not understand a word in a story, what can you do?
questions.why: Asking helps us learn.

questions.q: Match.
questions.why: We use all three when we listen.

questions.q: Why do stories stay alive when people listen?
o: Because they are very loud to hear
questions.why: Listeners become tellers.

panel.q: A friend tells a story and you were looking away. What did you miss?
o: Facial clues and parts of the tale
Nothing at all, because you can guess it
panel.why: We miss details when we do not look.

panel.q: Why might the teller pause?
o: To build interest and let us think
Because they forgot the whole of the story

panel.q: How can you show a teller you enjoyed the story?

teach.model: A good listener sits still and pays attention. Listen with ears and picture the story in your head. Afterwards ask who, where and what happened.

points.ask: What do you do in your head?

stages.title: Retelling a short story
stages.hook: Can you tell a story you heard to someone else in your own words?
explain: To retell a story means to tell it again. You do not need to say every word. Say who was in it, where it happened, and what happened first, next and last.
Use your own words. Add a little voice and make faces. Keep the order right.
Retelling helps you remember. It also keeps stories alive for new listeners.

example.q: Retell The Tortoise and the Hare in three steps.
steps: Beginning: a hare and a tortoise have a race.
Middle: the hare runs fast, then naps. The tortoise keeps going.
Ending: the tortoise crosses the line first.
example.a: The slow tortoise wins because he did not stop.

analogies.home: Tell your family what happened at school.
analogies.city: Tell a friend about your bus ride.
analogies.farm: Tell what the animals did today.
analogies.sea: Tell the story of a boat trip.

stages.mnemonic: Who, Where, First, Next, Last: five fingers to retell fast.
terms: To tell a story again in your own words.

misc.right: Retelling uses your own words, keeping the main events in order.

trip.prompt: Look for how storytellers keep an audience.

questions.q: What does retell mean?
o: Tell a story again in your own words
Hide the story away in a little box
questions.why: Retelling is telling again.

questions.q: Which should a retelling keep?
o: Only the last word of it
questions.why: Order keeps the story clear.

questions.q: Retell: put these in order.
items: The hare and tortoise start a race
questions.why: Race, nap, win.

questions.q: Which word starts a retelling?
questions.why: First begins the order.

questions.q: Do you have to use the very same words?
questions.why: Own words are fine.

questions.q: Ana forgets the middle when retelling. What may happen?
o: The listener will not know what happened
The story becomes a perfect one anyway
questions.why: The middle has the main events.

questions.q: Match the retelling word to its use.
questions.why: These words carry the order.

questions.q: Why add a voice and faces when you retell?
o: It makes the story fun to hear
It hides the plot from everyone
questions.why: Voice brings stories to life.

questions.q: Your friend retells a fable and leaves out the moral. What would help?
o: Add the lesson at the end
questions.why: The moral completes a fable.

questions.q: Why does retelling help us remember?
questions.why: Practice strengthens memory.

panel.q: Two children retell the same tale with different words but the same events. Are both right?
o: No, only one of them is right

panel.q: Why do tellers change a little each time?
o: They remember and adapt to listeners
They are lazy and do not really care

panel.q: What makes a retelling clear?
o: Who, where, and the order of events
A very loud voice and nothing more
Lots of new characters added in the end
panel.why: Clear parts give a clear story.

teach.model: To retell, say who was in it and where. Then tell first, next and last in your own words. Keep the main events in order. For example, retell the tortoise and the hare.

points.ask: Do you use the same words?
